\section[hodiē]{hodiē — today}

\label{lesson:LA-C103-hodie}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for inside, then the Latin for outside.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: hodiē}
\textbf{hodiē} — \textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{hōc diē}, \textquotedblleft{}on this day\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hodiē} is contracted from \emph{hōc diē}, \textquotedblleft{}on this day\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); \emph{diē}, \textquotedblleft{}on the day\textquotedblright{}, is a form of \emph{diēs}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[herī]{herī — yesterday}

\label{lesson:LA-C103-heri}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for outside, then the Latin for today.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: herī}
\textbf{herī} — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{herī} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*dhghyes-}, \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). An older \emph{*hesī} shows in \emph{hesternus}, \textquotedblleft{}of yesterday\textquotedblright{}, and English \emph{yesterday} is a cousin (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[annus, annī]{annus, annī — a year}

\label{lesson:LA-C103-annus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for today, then the Latin for yesterday.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: annus, annī}
\textbf{annus, annī} — \textquotedblleft{}a year\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{annual}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{annus} is inherited, usually traced through Proto-Italic \emph{*atnos}, \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}, to a Proto-Indo-European root \emph{*h2et-}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). Gothic \emph{aþn}, \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for today, then the Latin for yesterday, then say \emph{annus} again

\section[mēnsis, mēnsis]{mēnsis, mēnsis — a month}

\label{lesson:LA-C103-mensis}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for yesterday, then the Latin for a year.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mēnsis, mēnsis}
\textbf{mēnsis, mēnsis} — \textquotedblleft{}a month\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mēnsis} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*meh1ns}, \textquotedblleft{}moon, month\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{*meh1-}, \textquotedblleft{}to measure\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). English \emph{moon} and \emph{month} are cousins (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[aurōra, aurōrae]{aurōra, aurōrae — the dawn}

\label{lesson:LA-C103-aurora}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a year, then the Latin for a month.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aurōra, aurōrae}
\textbf{aurōra, aurōrae} — \textquotedblleft{}the dawn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aurōra} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*h2ewsōs}, \textquotedblleft{}dawn\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1); Greek \emph{ēōs}, \textquotedblleft{}dawn\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin (Lewis \& Short), and so is English \emph{east}.
\end{cousinweb}
